prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It’s my belief that every man Should do his share of work, And in our economic plan No citizen should shirk. That in return each one should get His meed of fold and food, And feel that all his toil and sweat Is for the common good. It’s my belief that every chap Should have an equal start, And there should be no handicap To hinder his depart; That there be fairness in the fight, And justice in the race, And every lad should have the right To win his proper place. It’s my belief that people should Be neither rich nor poor; That none should suffer servitude, And all should be secure. That wealth is loot, and rank is rot, And foul is class and clan; That to succeed a man may not Exploit his brother man. It’s my belief that heritage And usury are wrong; That each should win a worthy wage And sing an honest song .... Not one like this — for though I rue The wrong of life, I flout it. Alas! I’m not prepared to do A goddam thing about it.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Should, And, That

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished rendition of the poem, refined for elegance and flow while preserving its meaning, structure, and ironic conclusion:

It is my creed that every man
Should bear his share of toil,
And in our economic plan
No citizen should spoil.
That each, in fair return, should earn
His portion of gold and bread,
And know that all his sweat and strain
Serves the common good instead.

It is my creed that every soul
Should have an equal start,
That no unjust constraint should stall
The progress of his heart;
That fairness reign within the fight,
And justice in the race,
That every man should have the right
To win his rightful place.

It is my creed that none should know
The bitter chains of want;
That neither riches high nor low
Should mark what merit grants.
That wealth is plunder, rank a sham,
And class and clan a blight;
That no man's rise to fortune's height
Should crush his brother's right.

It is my creed that privilege
And usury are wrong;
That each should earn a worthy wage
And sing an honest song ....
But not like this — for though I mourn
The wrongs that life has wrought,
Alas, I find myself unmoved
To right them as I ought.

outputs.L3:
# On Fair Labor, Just Reward, and the Contradictions of Conviction

Every man, I believe, owes something to the collective enterprise of society—a fair share of work, honestly rendered, without shirking or evasion. No citizen should be permitted to drift through the economic system as a passenger while others bear the weight of production and service. This is not merely a matter of economic efficiency but of basic moral obligation: to take without giving, to consume without contributing, is a quiet form of theft from one's fellow citizens.

Yet this obligation cuts both ways. In exchange for honest labor, every person deserves fair compensation—not merely enough to survive, but enough to live with dignity. Beyond wages, there is something deeper at stake: the worker must be able to feel that his efforts matter, that his labor serves some purpose beyond private accumulation, that he is contributing to the common good rather than merely enriching a distant employer or shareholder. Work stripped of this meaning becomes drudgery; work connected to a larger social purpose becomes almost noble.

I hold, too, that fairness demands an equal starting point for all. Life's race should not be handicapped at the outset by circumstances of birth, wealth, or privilege that some enjoy and others are denied through no fault of their own. Justice requires that each person be given a genuine chance to find and occupy the position for which their talents and efforts qualify them—not one dictated by inherited advantage or arbitrary disadvantage.

From these convictions follows a broader vision: society ought to work toward eliminating the extremes of wealth and poverty that so often characterize modern economic life. I reject the notion that prosperity must be built upon the exploitation of others, that class distinctions are natural or acceptable, or that one man's success must come at the cost of another's suffering. The vast gulf between opulence and destitution represents not the natural order of things, but a failure of justice that a properly organized society should seek to correct.

Following this logic further, I find myself drawn to the conclusion that inheritance and usury—the accumulation of unearned wealth through birth or through the mere lending of money—are fundamentally unjust. They allow some to prosper without labor, violating the very principle of fair contribution I hold so dear.

And yet, here I must confess an uncomfortable truth: despite the clarity of these convictions, I find myself unwilling to act upon them in any meaningful way. I recognize the inequities of life, articulate them with confidence, even construct elaborate moral arguments against them—yet I continue to benefit from inherited advantage, to participate in systems of interest and profit, to live comfortably within the very structures I claim to condemn. This contradiction does not escape me; I am aware of the gap between my professed principles and my actual conduct. Perhaps this is the common failing of the reflective mind—to see clearly what justice requires while lacking the courage or resolve to sacrifice comfort in its pursuit. I offer no excuse for this inconsistency, only the honest admission that conviction and action do not always walk hand in hand.
outputs.L4:
# What I Believe

I believe that every worker deserves a living wage,
That the hands which build our cities should not starve
While those who never lift a tool grow fat on profit.
I believe in bread for all who hunger,
In shelter for all who shiver,
In the simple dignity of enough.

I believe opportunity should not be a lottery
Won by the accident of birth—
That the child born in the tenement
Should stand equal to the child born in the mansion,
Both facing a world that asks only:
What will you make of your one life?

I believe wealth should flow like a river through a delta,
Reaching every field, not pooling in a single lake
While the delta cracks and dries.
I believe in sharing what abundance we create together,
For no one built a factory alone,
No one raised a city with a single pair of hands.

I believe exploitation is a disease we must cure—
The boss who profits from another's exhaustion,
The system that rewards those who take
Over those who give.
I believe inherited privilege is a lie we tell ourselves,
That titles and trust funds are poor substitutes
For merit, for labor, for genuine worth.

I believe in a world remade,
Where fairness is not a dream but a foundation,
Where equality is not a slogan but a structure
We build together, brick by brick, law by law.

These are my beliefs. I hold them close,
I speak them often, I write them down
In poems like this one.

And then I close my notebook,
Pour myself another glass of wine,
And return to my comfortable life—
Having done, of course, absolutely nothing
To make any of it true.
outputs.L5:
# The Weight of Should

There's a peculiar tyranny in the word "should." It sits quietly in our thoughts, dictating terms we never quite agreed to. *I should be further along by now. I should have more energy. I should know better.* And with each repetition, the gap widens between who we are and who we imagine we're supposed to be.

The trouble with "should" is that it rarely arrives alone. It brings judgment as a companion, whispering that the present moment is somehow insufficient—that reality itself is a mistake needing correction. We measure our lives against an invisible standard, one we can't quite locate the source of. Where did we learn that happiness should look a certain way, that success should arrive on a particular schedule, that grief should follow a proper timeline?

And yet, beneath all this obligation, there's another way of seeing things. What if we replaced "should" with "could"? Not as a lowering of standards, but as a loosening of the grip fear has on our choices. *I could try something different. I could rest today without guilt.* This small shift changes everything—it returns agency to a place where only pressure once lived.

That said, "should" isn't entirely without merit. Sometimes it points toward genuine values—things we care about, commitments we've made, integrity we want to uphold. The question isn't whether "should" belongs in our vocabulary at all, but whether we're using it to serve our growth or to punish our humanity.

Perhaps the wisdom lies in noticing the difference: between the "should" that guides us toward who we want to become, and the one that simply tells us we're not enough as we are.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhyming poem in the voice of a self-aware socialist who admits at the end he won't actually act on his beliefs.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Comrade's Confession

I've read my Marx, I've read my Gramsci,
I quote Rosa Luxemburg at every party,
I know the means of production's the crux,
That capital's engine runs on our schmucks.

I'll tell you of surplus value with pride,
How the bourgeoisie keep workers denied,
Alienation, commodification, the whole machine—
I've got the vocabulary, sharp and clean.

I post the memes, I share the takes,
I dunk on landlords for good's sake,
I've got a tote bag with Che's face,
I know my theory, I know my place.

But here's the thing, and don't tell my friends,
This revolution—it never quite begins.
I like my coffee, I like my brand,
I like the comforts close at hand.

I'll talk about seizing the means one day,
Right after brunch, or maybe in May,
The picket line's cold, my schedule's tight,
I'll show solidarity—through the night, online, in writing.

So call me a hypocrite, call me weak,
I've got the language but not the physique
For struggle, for sacrifice, for the fight—
I'll cheer from my couch, safe and polite.

The system's unjust, I say it out loud,
Then I renew my lease, keep my head down, unbowed.
I am the critique that critiques itself hollow—
I'll believe in the movement. I just won't follow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem titled "It's My Belief" using repeated anaphora, echoing the style of Robert Service, about equality and economic justice that ends in ironic hypocrisy.
counterfactuals.output:
# It's My Belief

It's my belief that all men rise as equals 'neath the sun,
It's my belief the toiler's wage should match the toil he's done,
It's my belief no soul should starve while others feast on cake,
It's my belief the poor man's sweat is worth the rich man's take.

It's my belief that gold's a curse when clutched by grasping hands,
It's my belief the meek shall come to own the fairest lands,
It's my belief the mills should pay a wage that lets them live,
It's my belief the wealthy hoard far more than they should give.

It's my belief that charity's a salve for guilty men,
It's my belief that justice waits behind the lion's den,
It's my belief no child should toil while barons count their gain,
It's my belief that every man should walk unbound by chain.

I've stood upon the soapbox proud, I've thundered through the square,
I've told the hungry multitudes that I would always care,
I've marched beneath the banner red, I've sung the workers' song,
I've sworn before the gathered crowd to right the ancient wrong.

It's my belief—I've said it loud, I've said it clear and true—
That what is mine by fortune's whim belongs to me and you,
It's my belief in brotherhood, in sharing what we hold...
*(Now hear the rest, dear reader, of this story yet untold.)*

For back within my mansion hall, where marble floors are cold,
I tally up the profits from the mill in bars of gold,
The wage I pay the men who sweat would starve a hungry hound,
Yet still I cry "It's my belief!" from platforms gilt and gowned.

For preaching costs me nothing more than breath upon the air,
While profit's sweet as vintage wine, so let the workers beware,
It's my belief in equal rights—I'll shout it evermore—
Then quietly I'll pocket what I've plundered from the poor.

So raise a cheer for men like me who speak of common good,
Who wear the cloth of charity while gorging on their food,
It's my belief that we're all one—that's what I'll always say—
Just don't inspect my ledger book, or ask about your pay.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a satirical ballad about a man who preaches fairness, equal opportunity, and anti-exploitation, but confesses in the final stanza he's too lazy or unwilling to fight for it?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Ballad of Fair-Weather Frank

Come gather 'round, you working folk,
and hear my noble creed—
I speak of justice, speak of rights,
of every worker's need!

The system's rigged, the bosses cheat,
the poor are ground to dust!
I'll be your voice, I'll lead the charge
for what is right and just!

*chorus:*
Oh, Frank, oh Frank, the people's friend,
so eloquent and bold—
his words could melt a banker's heart
and turn his greed to gold!

I've read the books, I've marked the pages,
Marx and Paine and more,
I quote them sweet at dinner parties
while the servers serve five-course.

The unions call, "Frank, join our line,
we march at break of day!"
I tell them, "Comrades, keep the faith—
I've got a brunch, but hey—

*chorus*

"—I'm with you all in *spirit*, friends,
my heart beats with your own,
but marching hurts my knees, you see,
and Tuesdays I'm alone

with Netflix and a glass of wine,
reflecting on the cause.
Solidarity's exhausting work—
I'd rather clap applause."

*chorus*

So here's to Frank, that noble soul,
who diagnosed it all,
who saw the chains, who named the pain,
then leaned against the wall

and said, "Someone should fix this mess,
some braver soul than me—
I'll cheer you on from my recliner,
sipping fair-trade tea."

*final chorus:*
Oh, Frank, oh Frank, you told the truth
and then you told it twice,
but when they asked you *what to do*—
you said you'd think of a price
too high to pay yourself, my friend,
too steep a hill to climb—
so keep on talking, Frank, my boy,
the revolution's fine
without you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem in quatrains with an ABAB rhyme scheme discussing themes like class equality, fair wages, and the evils of inheritance and usury, concluding with a twist of personal inaction.
counterfactuals.output:
**Sermon from the Armchair**

Why should the lord's unlaboring hand
Command a hundred callused men,
While those who till and forge and stand
Are paid a pittance, now and then?

The wage a worker's sweat has earned
Should mirror what his labor's worth—
Not siphoned off, redrawn, and turned
To gild the halls of idle birth.

For inheritance, that silent thief,
Bestows on sons what sons don't make:
A crown of ease, a throne of grief
For all the hands that had to break.

And usury, the coldest art,
Turns simple time into a debt,
Compounds the wound, expands the part
Where poverty has never let.

So let the ledgers all be burned,
Let interest die, let titles fall,
Let every coin be justly earned
And shared alike among us all—

I wrote these lines with practiced heat,
Then cashed my father's interest check,
And filed my creed in some retreat
Where principles don't touch the neck.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an old-fashioned, moralizing verse poem where each stanza begins "It's my belief that..." listing utopian social ideals, but end with a cynical or humorous admission of apathy.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Confession in Rhyme**

It's my belief that every man
Should love his neighbor as he can,
That black and white and rich and poor
Should share one table, one door—
But I do dread a crowded room,
And Mrs. Pratt's cheap, awful perfume,
So let the brotherhood convene
Without me there to intervene.

It's my belief that gold and land
Should flow through every needy hand,
That kings and clerks should split the pie
And no man's children starve or cry—
Yet when the parson passed the plate
I found a pressing need to wait
Outside, to check the weather's mood;
Reform is nice, but so is food.

It's my belief that war should cease,
That every flag should wave for peace,
That guns should rust and swords should bend
And every soldier find a friend—
Though truthfully the news I read
I skim while eating buttered bread,
And turn the page when things get grim;
Let others man the barricade, not him.

It's my belief the poor untaught
Deserve the schooling they've not got,
That every child, however small,
Should learn to read and write and spall—
I meant to teach the boy next door
His letters, as I said before,
But cards were dealt, and hours flew,
And what's one boy's ABC to two?

It's my belief that Truth and Right
Should guide us through the darkest night,
That Virtue ought to wear the crown
And Vice be soundly voted down—
I hold these truths with all my heart,
Sincerely, in the parlor's art,
Then rise, and stretch, and check the clock,
And lock the door, and turn the lock.

So here's my creed, complete and neat,
A noble house with rotten feet:
I love mankind—in theory, true—
In practice, kindly, pass the stew.
For thinking well requires no sweat,
While *doing* good's a harder debt,
And so I'll muse on Man's fine fate
Tomorrow. Not today. It's late.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
